TargetRLF1: STI yɛ nyarewa a efi onipa biako hɔ kɔ foforo mu denam nna mu nkitahodi biara a ɛyɛ ɔbarima ne ɔbea nna a efi awotwaa mu, akyi berɛmo mu, anaa anom. STI ahorow a ɛtaa ba no bi ne chlamydia, gonorrhoea, syphilis, HPV (onipa papillomavirus), HIV/AIDS (nnipa nipadua mu nkwammoaa a ɛko tia nyarewa mmoawa), ne herpes. Sɛ obi nya STI a, obetumi ada sɛnkyerɛnne ne nsɛnkyerɛnne adi anaasɛ ɔrenkyerɛ sɛnkyerɛnne biara ntɛm ara. Sɛ ɛhaw wo sɛ ebia wowɔ STI a, ɛho hia sɛ wokɔ akwahosan adwumayɛbea a ɛbɛn wo no kɔyɛ nhwehwɛmu foforo. STI a Wobesiw Ano: Ɔkwan a wotumi de ho to so sen biara a wobɛfa so asiw STI ano ne sɛ wobɛtwe wo ho afi nna mu nkitahodi biara ho. Nanso, sɛ wo ne obi da a, fa kɔndɔm di dwuma. Sɛ wode kɔndɔm di dwuma a, ɛtew asiane a ɛwɔ hɔ sɛ wubenya STI ne nyinsɛn nso so. Kɔndɔm: Sɛ wode kɔndɔm (latex anaa polyurethane) di dwuma bere nyinaa na wode di dwuma bere nyinaa wɔ nna mu adeyɛ biara mu a, ebetumi atew asiane a ɛwɔ hɔ sɛ wubenya STI so kɛse. Dental dams: Dental dams yɛ plastic ahinanan a wɔde di dwuma bere a wɔde ano reda de ayɛ akwanside wɔ w’ano ne wo hokafo no hokafo awotwaa ntam. ɛtew asiane a ɛwɔ hɔ sɛ obi benya STI bere a wɔde ano reda no so. Nkitahodi: Wo ne wo hokafo (hokafo) nkasa pefee ne nokwaredi mu fa nna mu akwahosan ho nsɛm ne nhwehwɛmu a wobɛyɛ sɛ ebia wowɔ STI ho. Sɛ woyɛ nhwehwɛmu hu sɛ wowɔ STI a, ɛho hia sɛ wodi ayaresa no so na wowie na woma wo hokafo nso gye ayaresa. Vaccination: Vaccines betumi abɔ wo ho ban afi STIs binom te sɛ HPV ne Hepatitis B. Kɔ akwahosan asoɛe a ɛbɛn wo na wo ne mmabun akwahosan ho adwumayɛfo nkasa ma wɔnyɛ nhwehwɛmu ne vaccination.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection can cause serious problems if left untreated, particularly among women. Infants of mothers with Chlamydia can be infected at delivery and may result in eye infection (conjunctivitis) and pneumonia. The risk of complications may increase with repeated infections. Infection with chlamydia can cause stigma and affect personal relationships. These effects are important but often not quantifiable.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). These lesions burn and can be painful. They can appear on the buttocks, anus or thighs, on the vulva or vagina in women, and on the penis or scrotum in men. Often, before the lesions appear, patients describe a prodrome, characterized by a tingling or burning sensation in the area where the lesions will develop that can be noticed during urination, along with itching or discomfort in the genital area. You can also have the following symptoms, Blisters on the mouth or lips, Fever, headache or pain in the joints, Trouble urinating. In case of Neonatal Herpes, signs that your baby may have herpes are:irritability, blisters anywhere on her body, trouble breathing, grunting, blue appearance (cyanosis), rapid breathing, short periods of no breathing, jaundice, bleeding easily. People can have repeated outbreaks over time (‘recurrences’). These are usually shorter and less severe than the first outbreak. Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

TargetRLF1: A Urinary Tract Infection (UTI) and a Sexually Transmitted Infection (STI) are not the same.  A STI is an infection that is spread from one person to another through sexual intercourse. A UTI is infection of the bladder the kidney or the tubes connected to them. Bacteria that live in the genital and anal areas may move to the urinary tract and cause a UTI. Sexual intercourse can increase risk of getting a UTI if sexual activity introduces germs into your urinary tract but UTIs cannot be spread from one person to another. UTIs and STIs can also have similar symptoms such as fever, lower abdominal pain and pain on urination. Your healthworker will be able to do some tests to diffferentiate the two. A simple way to reduce your chances of getting a UTI is to urinate right after intercourse.

TargetRLF1: Chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary Infection often has no symptoms, but it can cause serious health problems, even without symptoms. If symptoms occur, they may not appear until several weeks after having sex with a partner who has chlamydia. In women, common symptoms of genital infection include: a change in vaginal discharge (white, yellow or grey discharge that may be smelly) , bleeding between menstrual periods or after sex, pain or discomfort in the lower abdomen and burning sensation when urinating. Common symptoms of genital infection in men include: burning when urinating, discharge from the penis (mucus-like or clear watery discharge), pain or discomfort in the testicles. Anal infection in women and men can cause: pain, mucus-like discharge and bleeding. If a patient has Lymphogranuloma Venereum (LGV), initial symptoms may include genital ulcers, followed by painful swelling of lymph nodes in the groin. If untreated, it can lead to severe complications such as rectal strictures.

Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: Gonorrhea is classified according to site or according to its responsiveness to treatment. According to site, there is urogenital, extragenital and disseminated gonorrhea. Urogenital Gonorrhea primarily affects the genital and urinary tract. Extragenital Gonorrhea occurs outside the genital area. It can infect the throat (from oral sex) or the rectum (from anal sex) or can manifest as an eye infection (gonoccocal conjuctivitis) in new born babies. Disseminated Gonococcal Infection is a more severe form where the infection spreads throughout the body. According to responsiveness to treatment, there is regular or multidrug resistant/super gonorrhea. Regular gonorrhea responds to commonly used antimicrobial drugs. However, multidrug resistant (super) gonorrhea is resistant to so many treatment options, including penicillins, sulphonamides, tetracyclines, quinolones and macrolides (including azithromycin), as well as so-called last line options like cephalosporins.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is a zoonosis – an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who'd died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream. Chimpanzees avoid humans wherever possible, so it is likely that SIVcpz crossed into humans as a result of human encroachment into forest areas. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs/wipes your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample and send it to a lab for testing. If bacteria are present, it indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: Syphilis develops in stages. The symptoms vary with each stage. But the stages may overlap. And the symptoms don't always happen in the same order. You may be infected with syphilis bacteria without noticing any symptoms for years. Primary syphilis: The first symptom of syphilis is a small sore called a chancre (SHANG-kur) that appears 2-12 weeks after exposure to someone with Syphilis. The sore is often painless. It appears at the spot where the bacteria entered your body. Most people with syphilis develop only one chancre. Some people get more than one. The chancre often forms about three weeks after you come in contact with syphilis bacteria. Many people who have syphilis don't notice the chancre. That's because it's usually painless. It also may be hidden within the vagina or rectum. The chancre heals on its own within 3 to 6 weeks. Secondary syphilis: While the chancre heals or a few weeks after it heals a Syphilis rash may develop; often unitchy, may appear rough, red, or reddish-brown and may be faint. It usually starts on the body's trunk, including chest, stomach, pelvis, back, and limbs. In time, it also could appear on the limbs, the palms of the hands and the soles of the feet. Besides the rash, other symptoms may include wartlike sores, hair loss, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, and fatigue. Symptoms of secondary syphilis may go away on their own. But without treatment, they could come and go for months or years. Latent syphilis: If you aren't treated for syphilis, the disease moves from the secondary stage to the latent stage. This also is called the hidden stage because you have no symptoms. The latent stage can last for years. Your symptoms may never come back. But without treatment, the disease might lead to major health problems, also called complications. Tertiary syphilis: After the latent stage, up to 30% to 40% of people with syphilis who don't get treatment have complications known as tertiary syphilis. Here, they may develop permanently damaged heart, brain, muscles, bones, and eyes. Congenital syphilis: Pregnant people who have syphilis can pass the disease to their babies. Unborn babies can become infected through the organ that provides nutrients and oxygen in the womb, called the placenta. Infection also can happen during birth. Newborns with congenital syphilis might have no symptoms. But without fast treatment, some babies might get sores and rashes on the skin, fever, a type of discolored skin and eyes called jaundice, not enough red blood cells (anemia), swollen spleen and liver, sneezing or a stuffed, drippy nose called rhinitis, bone changes, weight loss, and swollen lymph nodes. Later symptoms may include deafness, teeth problems, and saddle nose, a condition in which the bridge of the nose collapses. Babies with syphilis also can be born too early. They may die in the womb before birth, or they could die after birth.

TargetRLF1: Active TB can almost always be cured with antibiotics. For pulmonary TB, antibiotics are usually taken daily for six months. For people with TB in other parts of their body, treatment will last longer, perhaps up to 24 months. Latent TB can be treated with preventative treatment to stop it turning into active TB. This is always necessary for people with HIV to prevent TB causing illness and to cure it. It will be a similar course of treatment to active TB. It’s important that you take all the pills you are given because if you don’t, TB becomes resistant to the drugs, and is much harder to treat.

TargetRLF1: The only way to completely avoid STIs is to not have vaginal, anal, or oral sex. If you are sexually active, you can do the following things to lower your chances of getting Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes:•        Being in a long-term mutually monogamous relationship with a partner who does not have herpes.•        Using condoms the right way every time you have sex.Be aware that not all herpes sores occur in areas that a condom can cover. Also, the skin can release the virus (shed) from areas that do not have a visible herpes sore. For these reasons, condoms may not fully protect you from getting herpes. If your sex partner(s) has/have genital herpes, you can lower your risk of getting it if:•        Your partner takes an anti-herpes medicine every day. This is something your partner should discuss with his or her healthcare provider.•        You avoid having vaginal, anal, or oral sex when your partner has herpes symptoms (i.e., during an "outbreak").If you are pregnant and have genital herpes, prenatal care visits are very important. Some research suggest that a genital herpes infection may lead to miscarriage or make it more likely to deliver your baby too early. You can pass herpes to your unborn child before birth, but it more commonly passes during delivery. This can lead to a deadly infection in your baby (called neonatal herpes). It is important that you avoid getting genital herpes during pregnancy. Tell your healthcare provider if you have ever had a genital herpes diagnosis or symptoms. Also tell them about any possible exposure to genital herpes. If you have genital herpes, you may need to take anti-herpes medicine towards the end of your pregnancy. This medicine may reduce your risk of having signs or symptoms of genital herpes when you deliver. At the time of delivery, your healthcare provider should carefully examine you for herpes sores. If you have signs or symptoms of genital herpes at delivery, a 'C-section' is likely to occur.

TargetRLF1: HSV-1 is mainly transmitted via contact with the virus in sores, saliva or surfaces in or around the mouth. Less commonly, HSV-1 can be transmitted to the genital area through oral-genital contact to cause Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes. It can be transmitted from oral or skin surfaces that appear normal; however, the greatest risk of transmission is when there are active sores. People who already have HSV-1 are not at risk of reinfection, but they are still at risk of acquiring HSV-2. HSV-2 is mainly transmitted during sex through contact with genital or anal surfaces, skin, sores or fluids of someone infected with the virus. HSV-2 can be transmitted even if the skin looks normal and is often transmitted in the absence of symptoms. In rare circumstances, herpes (HSV-1 and HSV-2) can be transmitted from mother to child during vaginal delivery, causing neonatal herpes.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) can infect individuals of all blood types, and there is no specific blood group that is more susceptible to HIV infection than others. HIV primarily infects specific immune cells in the body called CD4+ T cells, and it does not have a preference for a particular blood group. HIV is primarily transmitted through contact with certain body fluids, including blood, semen, vaginal fluids, rectal fluids, and breast milk, that contain a high concentration of the virus. It's important to note that HIV does not directly interact with or target the antigens present on the surface of red blood cells, which determine an individual's ABO blood type (e.g., A, B, AB, O). Blood type antigens are not receptors for HIV infection. HIV is a virus that primarily targets the immune system, specifically CD4+ T cells, and over time, it can weaken the immune system, leading to a variety of health problems if left untreated. The risk of HIV infection is related to behaviors and practices that expose individuals to the virus, rather than their blood type.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

It is important that you take all of the medicine your healthcare provider gives you because untreated or improperly treated Chlamydia can lead to serious complications. Do not share medicine for chlamydia with anyone. Recommended drugs include Doxycylcine, Azithromycin, Levofloxacin and Amoxicillin. If the mother had a documented chlamydial infection during pregnancy that was untreated, presumptively treat the infant, even without confirmation of infection.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is a zoonosis – an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream. Chimpanzees avoid humans wherever possible, so it is likely that SIVcpz crossed into humans as a result of human encroachment into forest areas. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s. It came to global attention after doctors started receiving reports of rare cases of pneumonia, cancer and other illnesses in young gay homosexual men and injection drug users. Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

Over the decades, the disease has spread all over the world.

TargetRLF1: While some people with Genital Herpes or Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV), also known as herpes will never have any symptoms, other people can develop symptoms within a few weeks of being infected. Common oral herpes symptoms include blisters (cold sores) or open sores (ulcers) in or around the mouth or lips. Most people notice a group or cluster of blisters or ulcers (lesions). Herpes is a lifelong sexually transmitted infection, that cannot be cured. However, the number of outbreaks/recurrences may reduce over time.

The organism that causes the disease was first discovered in 1879 in Albert Neisser, hence the organisma being called Neisseria Gonorrhoea. The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications.. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Your need for testing depends on your personal risk for getting Chlamydia. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample. You should get tested regularly if you have unprotected sex with a new partner, multiple partners or a partner who has an STI. You should also get tested if you have symptoms or you are pregnant. Many people with Chlamydia don't have symptoms. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection.

TargetRLF1: Human immunodeficiency virus is an infection that originated in animals and passed into human hosts. It is closely related to the simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) found in chimpanzees in central Africa. To date, the earliest known case of HIV-1 infection in human blood is from a sample taken in 1959 from a man who died in Kinshasa in what was then the Belgian Congo. SIV probably entered the human population as a result of hunting chimpanzees. It is plausible that transmission could have occurred through a hunter being wounded and blood from a chimpanzee entering his bloodstream.  The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s.

The word Gonorrhea itself derives from the Greek, meaning "the flow of seed" (gono: seed, rhea: flow).

TargetRLF1: Herpes can only be diagnosed at a health centre. You cannot test for it at home or using radiological methods. When a person has active herpes lesions (a.k.a. blisters, sores, ulcers), your healthcare provider may diagnose genital herpes by simply looking at any sores that are present, or a swab can be taken and tests done that can detect the virus directly. The tests used include culture and Nucleic Acid Amplification Testing (NAAT). Both culture and NAAT tests can identify the specific herpes virus type someone is infected with, but NAAT methods are more sensitive. Culture can easily miss infections and give false negative results. Because a culture works by requiring virus that is active, if a lesion is very small, or is already beginning to heal, there may not be enough virus present for an accurate culture. Beyond 48 hours of the symptoms appearing, there is a risk of receiving a false negative test result. Viral culture is even less accurate during recurrences (positive in only about 30% of recurrent outbreaks). NAAT methods are the preferred method, with PCR as the most-widely used NAAT method. These tests are fast, accurate, and can tell if a person has HSV-1 or HSV-2. There is also less chance of a false negative result with NAATs. If sores are not present, a blood test may be used to look for HSV antibodies. Blood tests can be used when a person has no symptoms but has concerns about having Herpes. Blood tests do not actually detect the virus but look for antibodies.

TargetRLF1: Genital herpes or Herpes simplex virus (HSV), known as herpes, is a common infection that can cause painful blisters or ulcers. It primarily spreads by skin-to-skin contact. The infection can cause painful blisters or ulcers that can recur over time. Medicines can reduce symptoms but can’t cure the infection.Recurrent symptoms of both oral and genital herpes may be distressing. Genital herpes may also be stigmatizing and have an impact on sexual relationships. However, in time, most people with either kind of herpes adjust to living with the infection.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI) so as to get treatment. The origin of the Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) has been a subject of scientific research and debate since the virus was identified in the 1980s.

TargetRLF1: A chlamydia also known as Chlamydial Genitourinary infection test detects the bacteria that cause chlamydia, a sexually transmitted infection (STI). This test tells you if you have the chlamydia infection so that you can get treat treatment and avoid complications. Your provider takes a sample of urine or secretions from your vagina, penis or rectum and sends it to a lab for testing using a test called NAATs (short for nucleic acid amplification tests), which is very accurate and easy to take. Results are usually ready in a day. Less often, providers use a cell culture to test for chlamydia. In this case, your provider swabs your vagina, urethra or anus to collect a sample of fluid and cells. They send the cells to a lab to test. If bacteria are present, they will grow, which indicates an infection. Providers may choose this type of chlamydia test to detect infections in the anus. Or they may use a cell culture to see how chlamydia treatments are working. Because of the possibility of multiple sexually transmitted infections, all patients with any sexually transmitted disease (STD) should be evaluated for chlamydial infection. There are no risks involved with these tests. Rarely the results of the tests may be inconclusive or unclear and you may need to give another sample.
